About this citation

The Analects is a compiled record of sayings, not a work by Confucius. The common formula 'Confucius said' refers to a tradent whose words were assembled by later hands, and the book-and-chapter locator is what makes a passage findable in any edition.

Exact wording

English (as recorded here)
“The Master said: What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.”
Classical Chinese
“己所不欲，勿施於人。”

Eight characters. The English needs twice as many words because Chinese needs no subject, no tense, and no article; “what you do not want done to yourself” supplies all three.

Forms in circulation that differ

  • “Do not do unto others what you would not have them do unto you.”
  • “Do not impose on others what you yourself do not desire.”

Attribution notes

Analects 15.24, where it is Confucius' answer to Zigong's question about a single word to guide a whole life — the word given is shu, 恕, “consideration.” The same principle appears again at 12.2. It is the negative formulation of the golden rule, stated as a restraint rather than an injunction to act; the positive form (“do unto others…”) belongs to a different tradition and is not interchangeable with it.

About Confucius

Confucius (Kong Qiu, 551–479 BCE) taught in the late Spring and Autumn period amid the Zhou order’s political fragmentation. Born in the state of Lu, he briefly held local office and then spent years seeking rulers who would adopt ritual-based, virtue-centered government.

Interpretation

In the Analects ren is the virtue that makes someone fully human, and Confucius defines it differently for each questioner — here through the capacity to recognise others as like oneself. The formulation is negative in form (what you do not want, do not do), which makes it usable without knowing another person's desires in detail. It is a procedure rather than a sentiment, and it is meant to be applied in ordinary dealings rather than in exceptional ones.

Why it matters

The negative form is what makes it workable: you know what you want to avoid without having to guess what someone else wants.

Questions readers arrive with

What is the source of the quotation “The Master said: What you do not want…”?

“The Master said: What you do not want…” comes from The Analects, 15.24 (c. 5th–3rd century BCE (compiled)), attributed to Confucius.

What does Confucius mean by ethics?

Across 4 recurring voices here (notably Kwame Anthony Appiah and Simone de Beauvoir), ethics is framed through Africana Philosophy and Existentialism. Some passages define ethics; others warn how it fails; still others relocate it inside habit, community, or language. This passage enters that discussion through ethics.

Is the wording of this Confucius quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “The Master said: What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.” Forms in circulation that differ: Do not do unto others what you would not have them do unto you. / Do not impose on others what you yourself do not desire. The Classical Chinese reads “己所不欲，勿施於人。”

Is this quotation attributed correctly?

Analects 15.24, where it is Confucius' answer to Zigong's question about a single word to guide a whole life — the word given is shu, 恕, “consideration.” The same principle appears again at 12.2. It is the negative formulation of the golden rule, stated as a restraint rather than an injunction to act; the positive form (“do unto others…”) belongs to a different tradition and is not interchangeable with it.
